title: Note (Expenses): Angus Tyres Limited v Angus Council
text:
Lands Tribunal for Scotland

NOTE (Expenses)

Angus Tyres Limited (Applicant) against Angus Council (Respondent)

Disputed Compensation Subjects: 56-58 Ferry Street, Montrose

Introduction

[1] This note deals with motions for expenses by the parties following our opinion of 18 May 2023. In summary we found the applicant entitled to the value of the subjects in the agreed sum of £170,000, of which £17,000 remained to be paid. We refused the second claim for disturbance for loss of MOT profits, but allowed the second claim for disturbance for partial extinction of business and loss of goodwill in the sum of £92,250. We allowed the third claim for professional fees incurred prior to the tribunal application (12 December 2017) in the restricted sum of £1,000 for accountancy fees.

[2] We would deal with the motions for expenses on the basis of written submissions. The applicant seeks the expenses of the application on the sheriff court scale, an additional fee by way of an uplift of 100% applied to the solicitor’s fees; certification of Mr David Bell CA and Mr Steven Taylor FCCA as expert witnesses, and to sanction the cause as suitable for the employment of junior counsel. The respondent on the other hand seeks the expenses of the application against the applicant, seeks the certification of Mr Gerry McCluskey MRICS and Mr Greg Rowand CA as skilled witnesses for the respondent and to sanction the application as suitable for the employment of junior counsel; or alternatively to make a finding of no expenses due to or by either party.

Legislation

Land Compensation (Scotland) Act 1963

“ 11 Expenses.

(1) Where either—

(a) the acquiring authority have made an unconditional offer in writing of any sum as compensation to any claimant and the sum awarded by the Lands Tribunal to that claimant does not exceed the sum offered; or

(b) the Lands Tribunal is satisfied that a claimant has failed to deliver to the acquiring authority, in time to enable them to make a proper offer, a notice in writing of the amount claimed by him, containing the particulars mentioned in subsection (2) of this section;

the Lands Tribunal shall, unless for special reasons it thinks proper not to do so, order the claimant to bear his own expenses and to pay the expenses of the acquiring authority so far as they were incurred after the offer was made or, as the case may be, after the time when in the opinion of the Lands Tribunal the notice should have been delivered.

(2) The notice mentioned in subsection (1)(b) of this section must state the exact nature of the interest in respect of which compensation is claimed, and give details of the compensation claimed, distinguishing the amounts under separate heads and showing how the amount claimed under each head is calculated.

(3) Where a claimant has delivered such a notice as is mentioned in subsection (1)(b) of this section and has made an unconditional offer in writing to accept any sum as compensation, then, if the sum awarded to him by the Lands Tribunal is equal to or exceeds that sum, the Lands Tribunal shall, unless for special reasons it thinks proper not to do so, order the acquiring authority to bear their own expenses and pay the expenses of the claimant so far as they were incurred after his offer was made.

(4) The Lands Tribunal may in any case disallow the cost of counsel.

(5) Where the Lands Tribunal orders the claimant to pay the expenses, or any part of the expenses, of the acquiring authority, the acquiring authority may deduct the amount so payable by the claimant from the amount of the compensation, if any, payable to him.”

Lands Tribunal for Scotland Rules 2003 (SSI 2003 / 452)

Expenses

28. —(1) For the purposes of determining applications under Part 9 of the (Title Conditions (Scotland) Act 2003), expenses shall be determined in accordance with sections 97(4), 99(3) and 103 of that Act. In all other cases except those to which the provisions of section 11 of the Land Compensation (Scotland) Act 1963 apply …, the Tribunal shall deal in such manner with the expenses as in its discretion it thinks fit …

(5) Additional expenses at such rate as the Auditor taxing the expenses considers fair and reasonable shall be allowed for the employment of expert witnesses only where the Tribunal has certified the employment of such expert witnesses.”

Applicant’s submissions

[3] The applicant had sought compensation on the basis of extinguishment of its business and had been successful in that the tribunal awarded compensation on the basis of partial extinguishment of the business. The respondent’s position had always been based on the proposition that the business ought to have been relocated; it had never been its position that the compensation could be based upon partial extinguishment of the business.

[4] Turning to the additional fee, in terms of head (a) it was submitted that the case was complex and raised difficult questions. The claim involved the reasonable businessman test and there were complex financial issues. Both parties had instructed expert witnesses. In terms of head (b) the agents spent considerable time in preparation and presentation of the case which was an application of a somewhat rare nature. For head (c) there was a significant number of documents lodged by the parties and the respondent lodged productions very late in the proceedings. The applicant’s expert report had been sent to the respondent on 3 March 2020 but the latter did not provide the claimant with a report until August 2022 which caused significant additional documents to be lodged. In terms of head (d) the claimant’s solicitor is based in Arbroath, but the tribunal took place over several years, from Edinburgh. The proceedings were important to the client, as provided for by head (e) and related to the extinguishment of business at one of the applicant’s tyre depots which was of importance to the claimant’s business activities. Under head (f) the value of the claim was £820,000. In terms of head (g) significant correspondence and discussions took place resulting in a lengthy joint minute being lodged, which had taken significant time by the solicitor in negotiating and finalising.

[5] Turning to the witnesses, both Mr Bell and Mr Taylor could be certified as skilled witnesses due to their respective qualifications and the evidence which they gave. It was reasonable and proportionate to employ both witnesses. The respondent had also employed a specialist witness.

[6] It was submitted that it was appropriate to employ counsel and it was noted that the respondent had also employed counsel.

[7] In response to the respondent’s submissions, it was pointed out that the applicant had corresponded extensively with the respondent about documents being sought, and produced letters dated 29 August 2018, 10 September 2019 and 3 March 2020 seeking clarification and confirming compliance with orders. No replies were received by the respondent. Various explanations were given as to failures to meet the tribunal’s timetable on a number of occasions. There had been delays in complying with timetables but this was largely as a result of the respondent not intimating its expert report until August 2022 despite Mr Bell’s report having been intimated on 3 March 2020.

[8] It was accepted that the tribunal had a discretion as to the question of expenses and it was pointed out that at no stage had the respondent made an unequivocal offer in writing offering compensation.

[9] Reference was made to Purfleet Farms Limited v Secretary of State [2002] EWCA Civ 1430 that, in the context of the equivalent to the 1963 Act, more had been awarded than any unconditional offer by the respondent, since no offer had been made. Thus an applicant was entitled to its costs absent some “special reason” to the contrary. Nor had the respondent identified any abandoned issues, unnecessary adjournments or failings which had led to a substantial escalation of costs over and above what was reasonable for the claimant to incur. Reference was also made to Potter LJat para [36]:

“… exaggeration alone is not enough in the event of a large disparity between the sum claimed and the sum awarded. The matters as to which the Tribunal should have regard are (a) the reasons for that disparity and (b) the effect upon the conduct of the claim. As to (a) if the reasons are defensible, in the sense that there was a legitimate albeit unsuccessful argument put forward in support of the figure concerned, there can be no good reason to regard the claim as exaggerated in the pejorative sense necessary to justify a sanction in costs. As to (b) if, in any event the effect on the proceedings in terms of the time spent and the costs incurred in disposing of the issue or argument concerned is relatively insignificant, then again an adverse order is unlikely to be appropriate.”

[10] His Lordship further observed:

“37. Turning to the question of expert evidence, if the amount of the ‘exaggerated’ claim is based on the valuation, opinion and evidence of the claimant’s expert witness, it will rarely be appropriate in my view to make an adverse costs order against the successful claimant. Valuation is an inexact science. In any case where, by reason of the nature or features of the subject site and/or the state of the market in respect of sites with similar development, there is no close or obvious comparable available, there is bound to be legitimate room for argument and difference of opinion as to the validity or usefulness of a proffered comparable, whether by reason of its location, nature or proposed use. If the Tribunal concludes that, on examination, or as a result of argument, the comparison between the comparable relied on and the subject site is inapt or unhelpful, that should not ordinarily invite a penalty in costs on the grounds that its assertion or resultant discussion has taken up the time of the Tribunal unnecessarily.

38. In my view Mr Barnes is correct when he submits that, in such cases, disallowance of a proportion of the claimant’s costs will usually only be justified where the Tribunal is satisfied that (a) no competent valuer could reasonably have regarded the comparable as of real relevance or assistance in the valuation exercise; (b) as a result of its introduction and discussion, a significant amount of the Tribunal’s time has been wasted and the proceedings unduly prolonged; (c) no equivalent or near equivalent proportion of the proceedings has been spent dealing with issues unreasonably and unsuccessfully raised by the respondent; (d) the amount or proportion of costs disallowed is proportionate to the time wasted.”

[11] It was submitted that as the claimant relied upon the valuation opinion and evidence of an expert witness it would be inappropriate to make an adverse finding against the applicant.

[12] Reference was also made to Aberdeen DC v Emslie and Simpson Limited 1995 SC 264 and the passage of Lord Morison at p 266:

“… I am not persuaded that the expenses of a reference to determine the amount of disputed compensation for compulsory purchase should necessarily be treated in the same way and according to the same principles of those which apply to litigation in the courts. A person whose interest in land is under threat of compulsory acquisition is in an unenviable position. He is compelled either to exceed the acquisition or to take steps provided by the legislature to oppose it. If the order is confirmed, he has no option but to comply with it and to have the amount of compensation determined either by agreement, if he can secure it, or if not, by reference to the Tribunal within the statutory framework which is laid down for that purpose. In these respects it appears to me that he is in a different position from that of the ordinary litigant and my understanding is that, if a person unsuccessfully opposes confirmation of the compulsory purchase order, he is not ordinarily found liable for the expenses of the statutory procedures which are laid down for the hearing of his objection. In respect of these procedures the principles applying to expenses in the courts do not apply, and it seems to me that there is justification for the adoption of a similar practice in respect of the other procedures which are laid down for the determination of the amount of compensation after an order has been confirmed. It is to be observed in this connection that the statutory procedures include special provision relating to the expenses of a reference, to which I shall refer later, and to this extent at least the position is not the same as that which governs awards by the courts.”

[13] At p 269 he further stated:

“If the advance payment is disregarded, the appellants are left to rely on the fact that the sum awarded was very much less than that which had been claimed and that it excluded a large number of very substantial items upon which the total claim was based. In ordinary litigation the question whether such a consideration had any effect on expenses and, if so, what, is very much a matter for the exercise of the discretion by the court which has decided the case and appeals based on this kind of consideration are discouraged. There are some cases in which such feature may lead to a determination that there has been divided success and that expenses should be modified on that account. In most cases, however, it is perfectly reasonable that, having been put to expense of establishing a right which has been disputed, a claimant should put forward his claim on the maximum basis which he can reasonably support and should be entitled to the expenses of doing so if he has been successful in the general assertion of his right. The protection afforded to a defender in an ordinary action in which only the amount of an reward is an issue, in relation to liability for expenses arising from proof of any part of the claim for which he is ultimately found not to be liable, is the lodging of a tender. The same protection is afforded to an acquiring authority by s11 of the 1963 Act to which I have referred. In the absence of an offer equaling or exceeding the amount of the award, the Tribunal were fully entitled to hold, as they did, that ‘in the normal course the claimant’s would be found entitled to their expenses on the general principle that expenses follow success.’ The claimants were required to go to the Tribunal to establish that they were entitled to a substantially greater sum than that which they had been offered. The dispute which required the reference was the absence of agreement to what the acquiring authority proposed and the claimants were successful in the resolution of that dispute. The Tribunal were therefore entitled to regard the fact that the award exceeded by a substantial margin the compensation which had been offered as a major consideration bearing in expenses in the circumstances of the case. Their decision to that effect is not only one which lay within their discretion, particularly in view of the fact that the exclusion of certain large items of their claim depended on narrow and complex determinations of law on which the claimants could not reasonably have refrained from making submissions if they chose, as they did, not to accept the offer made to them.”

[14] In the light of this passage it was clear that a claimant “should” put forward a claim on the maximum basis which could be reasonably supported, and the claimants had been successful in their general assertion of their rights.

[15] The claimant also referred to the passage of the Lord President at p 271 where he said:

“On the broader issue as to the approach which should be adopted on the question of expenses of this kind, I am not satisfied that the position in cases of disputed compensation is the same which applies to litigation generally. It seems to me that the underlying principle in these cases is that the acquiring authority is liable to pay compensation to the owner or occupier of lands taken. The expenses of determining the amount of disputed compensation may be seen to be part of the reasonable and necessary expense which is attributable to the taking of the lands compulsarily be the acquiring authority. The principle which applies to litigation, as expressed by Lord President Robertson in Sherpherd v Elliott at page 696 and quoted by McLaren on Expenses at p 21, is that the cost of litigation should fall on him who caused it. The cost of determining the amount of disputed compensation would seem, according to this principle, to fall on the acquiring authority without whose resort to the use of compulsory powers there would have been no need for the owner or occupier to be compensated. That seems to me to be the proper starting point for an examination of the question of expenses in these cases. While I think that the Tribunal should be guided, in the exercise of the discretion which was given to it by rule 33(1) of the Lands Tribunal for Scotland Rules 1971, by the general rules as explained McLaren at p 21-23, particular account should be taken in these cases of the underlying principle – especially when questions arise as to what constitutes success and whether the proceedings were necessary.”

[16] Accordingly the applicant emphasised the underlying principle that the acquiring authority was to pay compensation and that the expenses of determining the compensation could be seen as part of the reasonable and necessary expense attributable to the taking of the lands. There was no reason why this principle should be departed from.

[17] It was further submitted that there had been extensive negotiations since 2013 to resolve the level of compensation, and at no time had the respondent made any unconditional offer of compensation to the claimants: the applicant had to raise the proceedings to vindicate its rights. It was accepted it would be open to the respondent to address the auditor in relation to the applicant’s right to expenses for particular parts of the process.

[18] In response to queries from the tribunal, and responses thereto by the applicant, it was pointed out that at no time prior to the motion for expenses had the respondent suggested that the applicant had not complied with s11(1)(b) and (2). The matter could have been raised at any time and the tribunal could have been addressed. The intimation of the applicant’s schedule of compensation and expert reports amounted to a detailing of the compensation sought, thus demonstrating compliance with the section. The respondent could have made a proper offer in the light of these. The respondent failed to make an interim payment for 90% of the value of the property until 23 January 2018, despite the tribunal application being made on 17 December 2017. The redundancy payments claim had not featured in the pleadings, and was not insisted in. The test for certification of skilled witnesses as applied by the courts was contained in rule 5.3 of the Act of Sederunt (Taxation of Judicial Expenses Rules) 2019 (SSI 2019/75).

Respondent’s submission

[19] The respondent referred us to s11 of the 1963 Act and rule 28 of the Tribunal Rules. In the context of s11(1) and (2) it was pointed out that the claim for total extinguishment of the Montrose business, as specified in the compensation schedule and pleadings, had been modestly sustained as one for partial extinguishment only. The upheld claim was materially different in kind. Appropriate notice in terms of s11(2) had not been given. It was also pointed out that the applicant had not made an unconditional offer in writing to accept a sum, equal or less than the sum awarded, in terms of s11(3).

[20] In the context of Aberdeen DC v Emslie & Simpson Limited, reference should now be made to rule 28 of the 2003 Rules as opposed to rule 33 of the 1971 Rules. We were also referred to para [36] of Purfleet Farms Limited v Secretary of State whereby the tribunal could have regard to a practice direction whereby in determining costs the tribunal could have regard to all circumstances including the conduct of parties, which included whether a party had acted reasonably in pursuing or contesting an issue and how a party had conducted its case, including whether a claim had been exaggerated. Reference was made to Hemcomp Limited v Birmingham City Council , Lands Tribunal9 April 2008, where by reliance on upon unsupportable evidence may justify refusing to award an applicant costs in respect of compensation in respect of a CPO. Reference was also made to Blakes Estates Limited v Government of Montserrat [2006] 1 WLR 297 whereby a claimant who had put forward a grossly excessive claim could be deprived of part of its costs if the exaggeration had given rise to an obvious and substantial escalation of the costs incurred, whereby the amount of any such reduction should be proportionate to the wasted time and costs properly attributable to the claimant’s acts and admissions.

[21] Reference was made to McLaren on Expenses pp25-30, as had been endorsed by the Lord President in Emslie & Simpson , where examples were given of where expenses may be awarded against a “successful” party, namely if he had conducted the litigation unreasonably or carelessly, his pleadings were deficient, he had failed to provide information or evidence, or where the successful party had been awarded only a small part of the claim. An award of expenses could be refused where the litigation had been conducted improperly or the court proceeded on grounds which had not been argued or pled. Expenses could be modified to mark disapproval where a successful party’s evidence had been unsatisfactory, the court had proceeded on grounds that were not pled, where matters were not admitted, where an admission would have shortened the hearing and where success had only been partial. A number of other cases were cited as examples where the court had awarded expenses against a pursuer who had only succeeded in obtaining a small sum as against a large conclusion.

[22] The respondent listed no less than ten examples where the applicant had been materially late in adhering to tribunal timetables and a draft timetable. The majority of these related to dates in the Autumn of 2022 in the run up to the evidential hearing. The respondent required to have the tribunal fix a hearing on account of the applicant’s failure to intimate witness statements for a large number of witnesses, which witness statements were finally lodged on 4 November, over 3 weeks late. The excuse for a late list of documents on account of Mr Rowand’s report not being lodged timeously was misconceived, since the report had been timeously lodged on 2 August 2022 in accordance with a draft timetable at that time.

[23] In general terms the applicant had exaggerated its claims; at one stage the total claims for loss of profits and value of goodwill amounted to £910,982; the tribunal quantified the business disturbance claim at £92,250, approximately 10% of what the applicant’s evidence had sought to justify. The claim was at all times grossly exaggerated. The applicant could not excuse this by reference to the fact the claim was a matter for expert valuation, since it was the information which had been provided to Mr Bell that was flawed.

[24] It was submitted there had been unreasonable failures to produce evidence. There had to be detailed prompting of the applicant to remedy deficiencies in the documentary evidence, by motions for commission and diligence, and in terms of Mr Rowand’s identification of large amounts of missing information in his report of 1 August 2022 which was disclosed to the applicant. There had been no trading records which could have permitted reliable identification of the turnover and earnings attributable to the Montrose depot; all there was were summaries which had been prepared for the purpose of negotiation with the respondent. No material was produced to permit a depot by depot comparison so as to assist to identify customers who continued to contribute to turnover and earnings. Despite the motions for recovery of evidence and Mr Rowand’s requests for information, there remained serious deficiencies in the evidence even by the close of the hearing, as had been noted by Mr Rowand and by the tribunal in numerous passages, which was an unreasonable manner to conduct litigation.

[25] It was submitted there had been concealment of material facts. There had been substantive exaggeration in that the applicant had pled it was entitled to compensation for the complete extinguishment of business at the Montrose depot. The claim had made no allowance for the survival of trade via other depots after closure of the Montrose depot. The fact that there had been a part transfer of business to the other depots was in effect concealed by the applicant. It was only first admitted by Mr Bell in his supplementary report dated 13 October 2022 (and lodged late) which matter had been discussed by the tribunal in their opinion. As the tribunal had identified, it was only once Mr Rowand had seriously scrutinised the claim by seeking information as to the applicant’s top ten customers that the applicant conceded the retention of a major customer namely Tayside Contracts. This must have been within management’s knowledge but Mr Bell appeared to have been informed otherwise: references was made to the tribunal’s opinion at para [217]. The claim had been deceptive which was unreasonable conduct.

[26] Another issue was that the respondent had been successful in persuading the tribunal that the applicant had failed to take reasonable steps to mitigate its loss by surrendering the Balmain Garage site. This led to a massive abatement of the claim.

[27] Another factor was that the MOT earnings claim had failed, and had not been pled. The respondent had nevertheless been required to investigate and respond to the claim which would have added at least one day to the hearing of the case.

[28] The applicant had claimed compensation for redundancy payments for four employees. Reference was made to a “record”, supplied by the applicant before the hearing, late and with pages missing, which appeared to incorporate the compensation schedule, making reference to prospective redundancy payments. The respondent had to investigate this part of the claim. In the event no evidence was led that any employee had been made redundant, and no submission was made for compensation in that respect. This was one of a number of omissions which was inconsistent with the claim for complete extinguishment of the business. It was unreasonable to have made such a baseless claim.

[29] The claim for professional costs had not been vouched and the tribunal had found this to be inexplicable. The respondent nevertheless had required to investigate the claim. The quantification of £1,000 was less than 2% of the compensation sought.

[30] Time had been pervasively taken up by the need to address aspects of the claim which were unpled, unsubstantiated by evidence, concealed or grossly exaggerated. Had the claim been presented as the modest one which it in fact was, it was plausible there would have been no dispute at all. No reasoned offer could be made because the applicant’s claim was evidently exaggerated, but the nature of any loss was necessarily a matter as to which it, the applicant, had special knowledge, and not the respondent.

[31] Turning to the motion for an additional fee, the value of the claim had in fact been quantified at £92,250, which was not a value justifying an additional fee. One critical consideration on whether an additional fee should be justified was the steps taken with a view to settling proceedings. It was submitted that pleading and seeking to prove over days of evidence a claim which had been exaggerated by a factor of roughly 10 is so grossly the antithesis of taking such steps, that the tribunal should consider that that alone suffices to rebut any claim for an additional fee.

[32] In any event the certification of Mr Steven Taylor as an expert witness should be refused. The matter should be governed by the Tribunal rule 28 and common law applicable to expert opinion.

[33] As a director of Murray Taylor Limited, chartered accountants, he had for many years been engaged as the applicant’s accountant. He was not an independent or impartial expert who could provide objective opinion evidence for the assistance of the tribunal: cf Kennedy v Cordia (Services) LLP [2016] UK SC 6 at paragraphs 44 and 51 ‑52, followed in CTIL v Fotheringham LTS/ECC/2020/0007. Moreover he had done nothing by way of preparing or providing expert evidence, he had been involved in providing financial documents to Mr Bell and to the tribunal and the respondent. He only narrated the steps he had taken, rather than give independent, expert evidence. This was not a case of tendering expert evidence to the tribunal. The respondent did not object to Mr David Bell being certified as an expert witness.

Discussion

[34] We recognise that the rules as to expenses of a tribunal application in land compensation cases are somewhat different to normal litigation. The tribunal may require to consider s11 of the 1963 Act, if the provision is applicable. This may or may not involve the exercise of a discretion depending upon whether special reasons are put forward for not applying the burden of sub‑paragraphs (1) and (3). Otherwise, absent s11 circumstances, the proper starting point for an examination of the question of expenses is the principle that the cost of determining the amount of the disputed compensation would fall on the acquiring authority without whose resort to the use of compulsory powers there would have been no need for the owner or occupier to be compensated: Aberdeen DC v Emslie & Simpson Lord Hope p 271. In the normal course, where a claimant has received an award beating a lower offer by a respondent, it will be found entitled to expenses on the general principle that expenses follow success: Lord Morison p 269 and Purfleet paragraph 19.3. As we shall discuss further below, there is specific guidance in compensation cases where there are questions of divided success and issues about the conduct of parties.

[35] The claimants refer to s11(1) and (2) of the 1963 Act. In short, these provisions require an applicant to provide a notice in time to enable the acquiring authority to make a “proper offer”. The notice should specify “the exact nature of the interest in respect of which compensation is claimed, and give details of the compensation claimed, distinguishing the amounts under separate heads and showing how the amount claimed under each head is calculated”. Failure in these matters will require, unless for special reasons the tribunal thinks proper not to do so, the claimant to be ordered to bear its own expenses and to pay the expenses of the acquiring authority insofar as they were incurred after the time when in the opinion of the tribunal the notice should have been delivered.

[36] Here the respondent points out that the claim insofar as modestly sustained was one for partial extinguishment, as opposed to a claim for the complete extinguishment of the Montrose business. Thus, it was argued, a claim was upheld materially different in kind to what was pled and argued, of which notice had not been given. The applicant had also failed to plead a claim for the lost MOT business.

[37] The extinguishment claim as presented in the compensation schedule of December 2017, and Mr Bell’s first report dated March 2020, assumed the applicant would lose, or had lost the total business carried on at the Montrose site: eg para 2.14 of the latter document. Mr Bell’s report was detailed and included discussion of the possibility of retained trade, before excluding it. After the respondent’s forensic accounting expert Mr Rowand interrogated the claim, Mr Bell’s supplementary report of 13 October 2022 conceded that a sum of up to £140,000 of “Montrose turnover” remained with the applicant via other depots: para 3.10.

[38] Accordingly we consider there is some merit in the respondent’s argument that at the point of intimation of Mr Bell’s supplementary report – 18 October 2022 – the claim was adapted from a total extinguishment claim to a partial extinguishment claim for the Montrose business. Although we do not think the nature of the claim was radically changed – essentially the claim was being modified - there is some force in the point that the “exact nature of the interest” in respect of which compensation was sought, had not been provided in terms of s11(2) until the intimation of the supplementary report. We are less convinced that it follows, in terms of the statute, such defect in specification alone resulted in the respondent being disabled from making a “proper offer.” It is true the respondent was unaware of an important concession until a fairly late stage in the case. But as we shall discuss there were inherent difficult issues in valuing the claim both in respect of the retained trade issue as well as other issues, irrespective of the terms of a notice of claim. On any view the case would require detailed recovery and review of accounting records and forensic accounting analysis in order to reach a realistic valuation.

[39] It is also the case that the compensation claim schedule intimated before the commencement of proceedings did not include the lost MOT business claim, which only appears to have been advanced in terms of Mr Bell’s first and subsequent reports. This matter does not appear to be as significant as the respondent contends. That it should have been pled formally appears to have been overlooked by the applicant, but there is no question that the respondent had notice of and had been able to deal with it in detail during the critical phase of the litigation.

[40] We are therefore not persuaded that s11 applies in these circumstances. It is therefore appropriate for us to consider expenses issues more generally.

[41] It is the case that very significant parts of the claim failed for reasons other than the retained trade issue discussed above. As we have indicated, the loss of MOT profit claim was only intimated in Mr Bell’s first report, and was not pled formally. Nevertheless that claim failed not for pleading reasons as such, but on grounds of remoteness. This involved an examination of the relevant law, and findings based upon circumstances of the applicant’s business during the shadow period, and in particular the steps taken at the time to invest in the MOT aspect of the business.

[42] A large amount of the business extinguishment claim failed on the basis of the application of the reasonable businessman test in the context of mitigation of loss. The applicant’s position in this matter, involving as it did the acquisition of the BGL premises in Montrose, had something of a tactical flavour. Nevertheless we accept that the applicant was in a genuine dilemma as to whether it could and should relocate the Montrose business, and ultimately the respondent was responsible for the creation of this dilemma.

[43] It seems to us that both these aspects of the claim depended, as Lord Morison has described it, upon narrow and complex determinations of law and, in our view, detailed analysis of facts. In our view these parts of the claim as submitted can properly be described as a claim being put forward on the maximum basis which could be reasonably supported. Thus the claimant should be entitled to the expenses of doing so if it is successful in the general assertion of the right. The applicant has been successful in that general assertion, and so we do not think it appropriate that “divided success” should result in modification by reason only that some components of the claim, albeit very large ones, have failed. As explained in Purfleet, it is necessary to understand the reasons why certain parts of the claim failed and, in our opinion, most of the components of the claim had some basis such that could not be described as “unreasonable” in the necessary sense.

[44] The respondent has made many points as to the reasonableness of the applicant’s conduct. We consider that the question of disclosure of retained trade is the most significant, and this matter is related to the s11 point. In this context we bear in mind the view of the Privy Council in Blakes Estates Limited v Montserrat, applying Purfleet at para 25:

“A claimant should prima facie be entitled to his full costs of preparing and presenting his claim. The Board of Assessment’s discretion to reduce the award from the payment of full costs should be exercised judicially. If it holds that the claim was grossly excessive, it is necessary for the Board then to inquire whether the exaggeration gave rise to an obvious and substantial escalation in the costs over and above those which it was reasonable for the claimant to incur. If it is satisfied that this was the case, then it is open to the Board to exercise its discretion to deprive the claimant of part of his costs. The amount of departure from full payment of the claimant’s costs should be proportionate, having regard to the amount of waste of time and costs properly attributable to the claimant’s acts or omissions.”

[45] Critically, the existence of retained trade ought to have been known to those managing the applicant, as we commented at para [217] of our opinion. This was a fact peculiarly within the knowledge of the applicant, and we accept it was only through the painstaking requests for information by Mr Rowand which led to its being uncovered. The failure to disclose this feature of the claim can, we think, be described as exaggeration “in the pejorative sense” as put by Potter LJ in Purfleet at para 36.

[46] Another significant reason for the difference between the amount claimed and the actual award related to the selection of the EBITDA percentage to turnover. There were substantial differences in parties’ respective approaches to valuation. At the heart of the problem was understanding why the cost allocations to the Montrose depot appeared to be so much less than for the other depots. Although we had some concern as to the late stage at which at least part of the explanation for the difference was offered (para [231] of opinion) we are unable to conclude that this aspect of the case involved exaggeration in the pejorative sense. For example, the excessive staff head count in Arbroath for 2014 and 2015 did not appear to impact directly upon the extrapolated figures for Montrose, and it was the Montrose figures which formed the basis of the applicant’s case.

[47] We now turn to the efficiency of the process. While not all the deadlines which the respondent details were missed by the applicant, or missed by much, our impression is that all too many timetable dates were allowed to pass without any attempt to seek an extension before they passed, and with an appropriate explanation. Perhaps the most egregious were that productions were three or four weeks late and the witness statements were three weeks late. A hearing for a motion intimated on 2 November 2022 had to be fixed, a week before the evidential hearing, at the instance of the respondent, in order to determine whether the hearing could proceed on account of the applicant’s failure to produce witness statements. Cases of this nature require documents and reports to be produced in stages, for due consideration and response by the opponent, and when this does not occur there will be knock on effects. This was the case in that on the first day of the hearing important late productions emerged and nearly two hours was lost arguing about whether they should be admitted. Although both sides sought to lodge productions, the documents related to extrapolated depot accounts whose absence Mr Rowand had criticised, and which he had been calling for, and which in our view should have been produced by the applicant much earlier. We do not accept the applicant’s principal explanation, namely that Mr Rowand’s main report was produced late. That report was produced timeously on 2 August 2022 in accordance with what at that time was a draft timetable.

[48] Drawing the threads together, we think that in general terms the applicant should be found entitled to expenses, subject to specific modification where this is warranted as proportionate to a particular failing. Firstly, the applicant has been successful in general terms. The fact that s11(3) was not invoked by an applicant’s lower or equal offer to settle does not alter this basic conclusion, in the light of the above authorities. Secondly, the respondent could have made an offer, based upon similar methodology to that used by the Tribunal. In the light of Mr Bell’s supplementary report, and indeed Mr Rowand’s sceptical first report, it would have been possible for the acquiring authority to formulate a broad approach to deal with the contentious issue of the amount of retained trade. On account of the poor quality of the disclosure and evidence as to the extent of retained trade, the tribunal made cautious, and perhaps very cautious, assumptions as to the loss of the Montrose business. These cautious assumptions will have worked against the applicant in that there is the potential to have significantly undervalued the claim if it been presented with more rigour. Similarly, we made cautious assumptions in our estimates of EBITDA. So the lack of transparency in the applicant’s claim has already been reflected in the conservative nature of the award. The respondent could have made an offer to settle the extinguishment claim on an equally conservative basis, in the knowledge there had been no or limited disclosure of the retained trade, but chose not to do so.

[49] Thirdly, it is the case that the extent of the retained trade and late intimation thereof was only one factor in the overall equation for the valuation exercise of the extinguishment claim. In reality the underlying basis of the case was not changed, but only modified in the light of the disclosure. The details of the claim had been under discussion and scrutiny for years. Inherent in the nature of the claim is that the accounts and financial records will require detailed scrutiny, and we can infer this would have been a time consuming exercise with or without disclosure of the retained trade. Had for example Mr Bell’s main report disclosed retained trade, we doubt this would have led to any reduced scrutiny by Mr Rowand, or reduced much time taken in the legal process. There would still have been required an exercise of examining, for example, the “before” and “after” top customers which had previously used the Montrose depot, as well as a time consuming examination of all the other contentious issues.

[50] As we have indicated, the claim in principle was successful, and the reasons why certain components of the claim were unsuccessful does not mean that those other components had been unreasonably advanced. Given the number of difficult issues inherent in the case, and the fact that the respondent chose not to make an offer to settle, we are unable to conclude that the failure to describe the claim as one of partial extinguishment, and to disclose the retained trade, significantly prolonged the litigation. If it were necessary to find special reasons not to apply the burden of s11(1) against the applicant, we think such reasons accordingly exist.

[51] We think the most proportionate way to deal with our conclusions on these matters is to find the applicant entitled to the expenses of the Tribunal application, subject to the following express modifications. We shall find no expenses due to or by either party for the first day of the hearing on 10 November 2022. The loss of nearly half the day dealing with late productions was largely due to the failure of the applicant to release documents according to the timetable, and to respond in good time to Mr Rowand’s many criticisms and requests for information. Thus large exchanges of information only occurred shortly before the hearing. While we cannot attribute specific costs due to the late disclosure of the retained trade, this was no doubt one of many factors exacerbating the rather chaotic scene on day one of the hearing. We shall also find the applicant liable to the respondent in expenses occasioned by respondent’s motion seeking disclosure of witness statements, which motion had to be intimated on 2 November 2022.

[52] We now turn to the motion for an additional fee for the applicant’s solicitor. We have had regard to para 5.2 of the 2019 Act of Sedurunt. We bear in mind that inasmuch as the case was complex and comprised many documents, the applicant had instructed counsel and a forensic accountant. On the other hand the sum not unreasonably sought was a large one. There was a lengthy joint minute which required to be ratified, but our impression is that the joint minute did not go much further than agreeing formal matters and basic history, as we would normally expect in such cases. The experts themselves usefully prepared a joint report showing areas of agreement and disagreement.

[53] In our view the case is borderline for attracting an additional fee. The rules permit an additional charge where one is justified to reflect the responsibility undertaken by the solicitor in the conduct of the proceedings. This presupposes that the solicitor’s conduct was equal to the additional responsibility. In this respect we are not persuaded that this was the case. We think the solicitor has to bear responsibility for significant failures to adhere to the timetable, and if matters were outwith his control to communicate effectively when deadlines would be missed and to explain why. This has added to the cost of the litigation and the burden upon both the respondent and the Tribunal. In these circumstances we shall refuse the motion for an additional charge.

[54] We now turn to the certification of expert witnesses. The respondent does not dispute certification of Mr David Bell CA as an expert witness who was led as an independent expert.

[55] Turning to the involvement of Mr Steven Taylor FCCA , it is the case that the tribunal’s rule 28(5) for certifying expert witnesses is in general, non-prescriptive terms. We think it appropriate to have regard to the modern approach of the court under para 5.3 of the Act of Sederunt which refers to the certification of skilled persons. The court requires to be satisfied whether the person in question is a skilled person and whether it was reasonable and proportionate that the person should be employed.

[56] Mr Taylor is a certified accountant. He is the applicant’s accountant. He had been involved in the negotiation process, and had prepared valuations for that purpose. His duties had included providing financial information initially to the Tribunal under recovery procedures, and latterly to the forensic accountants. One important part of his work was extrapolating accounts between individual depots for certain years for the purposes of the claim. This was not something which happened as a matter of course in the preparation of the applicant’s normal business accounts, since the latter did not distinguish between depots, but the work was needed specifically for the analysis of the claim.

[57] The respondent points out that Mr Taylor was not engaged as an independent expert witness, which according to counsel is what the tribunal rules envisage. We agree that he was not being led as an independent expert. He was not, for example, asked to offer an opinion as to his valuation of the business, and had he sought to do so, such evidence would no doubt have been objectionable. His work of extrapolating the performance of individual depots from the accounts was perhaps borderline, in that a judgement was required in order to make any apportionment in the accounts, but our understanding of the evidence was that this was a judgement which ultimately came from his client.

[58] However, we do not think it follows that Mr Taylor was not a skilled person or that it was not reasonable to employ him in support of the case. On the contrary, his work in supplying financial information, and preparing the breakdown accounts for the purpose of the claim, was necessary, not least so that the claim could be scrutinised. The work had the benefit of his being familiar with the business. Accounting skill was required. So we think that it was reasonable and proportionate to employ him in the tribunal application. We think that not to certify Mr Taylor, so that the auditor would be unable to allow his usual charges, would risk offending the principle of equivalence. So giving the tribunal rules a broad interpretation we shall certify Mr Taylor as an expert witness in the “skilled person” sense.

[59] There was no dispute that we should sanction the employment of junior counsel.

Conclusion

[60] We shall allow the applicant its expenses of the tribunal application on the sheriff court scale, as modified for the two matters referred to in para [51] above. We shall sanction the employment of Mr Taylor and Mr Bell as expert witnesses, and sanction the case as suitable for the employment of junior counsel. We shall refuse the motion for an additional fee.
